title: Level 1 project: a record keeper
lesson:
Time to put Level 1 together, the way CS50 ends each part with a problem set that's a real program. You'll build the **core of a record keeper** for harvests (or anything: attendance, sales, stock), as functions, so it's testable and could later get a window or a phone screen on top (that's what the Library's Farm log is).

What it needs:
1. `add(records, crop, kg)` adds a record dict `{"crop": ..., "kg": ...}` to the list, tidying the crop name (strip, lowercase) and refusing bad data: raise `ValueError` if kg isn't a positive number or the crop is empty.
2. `totals(records)` gives kg per crop as a dict.
3. `top(records, n)` gives the n crops with the most kg, as a list of (crop, kg) pairs, biggest first.
4. `save(records, path)` and `load(path)` write and read the records as lines like `maize,40` (load of a missing file gives an empty list).

Plan before you type: write the four function headers with a comment each, then do them one at a time, checking as you go. When it passes, write a few lines in `if __name__ == "__main__":` that use it as a little menu program. That's your first real program, with tests.

After this: **Level 2** (data and structure: classes, modules, testing your own code) when it's ready.

notes: One hint for the hardest part: sorted with a key sorts the pairs by their kg, biggest first, then [:n] keeps n of them.

exercises.title: The record keeper
exercises.prompt: Write add, totals, top, save and load as described in the lesson. All the tests must pass, including hidden ones about bad input and missing files.

tests.check:
r = []
add(r, " Maize ", 40)
add(r, "beans", 12)
add(r, "maize", 25)
assert r[0] == {"crop": "maize", "kg": 40}, r[0]
assert totals(r) == {"maize": 65, "beans": 12}, totals(r)
tests.name: add and totals

tests.check:
import os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "r.txt")
r = []
add(r, "maize", 40)
add(r, "beans", 12.5)
save(r, p)
assert load(p) == r, load(p)
tests.name: save and load give back the same records
missing file
tests.hint_if_fail: load() of a file that doesn't exist should return [] (try/except FileNotFoundError).

tests.name: refuses bad data
tests.hint_if_fail: Empty crop, negative kg or kg that isn't a number must raise ValueError and add nothing.

tests.check:
import os, tempfile
p = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "r.txt")
save([{"crop": "maize", "kg": 40}], p)
assert type(load(p)[0]["kg"]) in (int, float), "kg should load back as a number"
tests.name: numbers come back as numbers

hints: Do add first: crop = crop.strip().lower(); check isinstance(kg, (int, float)) and kg > 0 and crop; else raise ValueError.
save: one line per record, f"{r['crop']},{r['kg']}\n". load: split each line on the comma and convert kg with float (int if it's whole).
top: sorted(totals(records).items(), key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)[:n]

quiz.q: Why build the record keeper as functions instead of one long script?
choices: Each part can be tested and reused (a window or phone app can sit on top)
Runs that part only when you run this file directly, not when another file imports it
quiz.why: It's how a file can be both a tool and a library.

quiz.q: Before typing a bigger program, you should…
choices: Start at the top and keep going
Plan the parts (function headers and what each does), then build and check one at a time
quiz.why: Plan, then one piece at a time.

cards.q: Sort pairs by their second value, biggest first?

cards.a: try/except FileNotFoundError: return an empty result.
Code that runs only when the file is run directly.

explain: Explain level 1 project: a record keeper to someone who has never programmed, in your own words, with an example you make up (not one from the lesson).
